topics.name: Socialisation and the creation of social identity

questions.q: Primary socialisation happens mainly through…
questions.why: It is the first stage of learning norms and values, in early childhood.

questions.q: Norms are…
o: shared expectations about how to behave in a situation
questions.why: Values are broader beliefs about what is important.

questions.q: What is primary socialisation?
o: Learning from the media as an adult
Learning the basic norms and values of society in early childhood, mainly from the family
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many answers did not focus on primary socialisation.

questions.q: A child raised with almost no human contact cannot speak or behave in socially expected ways. Sociologists use such cases as evidence that…
o: human behaviour is mainly fixed by instinct
language develops naturally without other people
human behaviour is largely learned through socialisation
questions.why: Without socialisation, children do not acquire language or the norms of their culture, which suggests behaviour is learned rather than innate.

questions.q: A young British Asian follows family religious traditions at home but mixes them with Western music and fashion with friends. Which concept best describes this?
questions.why: A hybrid identity combines elements of more than one culture to create a new, mixed sense of self.

long.q: Explain what is meant by socialisation, referring to two agencies of socialisation.
scheme: B1: the process of learning the norms and values of a culture
B1: primary socialisation, e.g. the family, in early childhood
B1: secondary socialisation, e.g. school, peers, the media, religion
B1: explained how one agency transmits norms, e.g. sanctions, role models

long.q: Describe two forms of social control.
scheme: B1: formal social control: by agencies with official power to enforce written rules, e.g. the police, courts, schools
B1: described: e.g. laws backed by punishments such as fines or prison
B1: informal social control: through everyday reactions of family, peers and community
B1: described: e.g. positive sanctions (praise) and negative sanctions (disapproval, gossip, exclusion)

long.q: Explain two ways in which gender identity may be shaped by socialisation.
scheme: B1: a first way, e.g. canalisation in the family: children channelled towards 'gender-appropriate' toys and activities (Oakley)
B1: explained: children internalise these expectations as part of who they are
B1: supported with evidence or an example, e.g. manipulation: praising girls for appearance, boys for toughness
B1: a second way, e.g. the media providing stereotyped role models
B1: explained: repeated images normalise gender norms that young people copy
B1: supported with evidence or an example, e.g. advertising aimed separately at boys and girls, or studies of magazines and social media

long.q: Evaluate the view that human behaviour is shaped more by nature than by nurture.
scheme: B1: the nature view: behaviour is biologically determined (instincts, genes, sociobiology)
B1: the nurture view: behaviour is learned through socialisation
B1: evidence for nurture: feral and isolated children lack language and social norms
B1: evidence for nurture: cultural variation, e.g. Mead's study of gender roles in three New Guinea societies
B1: evidence for nature: some universal traits; twin studies suggest some traits are partly heritable
B1: criticism: feral cases may involve prior disability or abuse; Mead's research has been challenged
B1: an interactionist view: biology and socialisation work together
B1: a reasoned judgement, e.g. sociologists stress nurture because biology cannot explain variation across cultures and over time

long.q: Explain two ways in which ethnic identity may be maintained among minority ethnic groups.
scheme: B1: a first way, e.g. religion: places of worship, festivals and rituals
B1: explained: shared practices reinforce belonging and pass values to the next generation
B1: a second way, e.g. language spoken at home and taught in community schools
B1: explained: language carries cultural meanings and marks the boundary of the group
B1: recognises change: younger generations may form hybrid identities (e.g. Johal's 'Brasian')
B1: supported with a further example or evidence, e.g. family expectations, media from the country of origin, or responses to racism strengthening identity

questions.q: Interpretivists prefer methods that…
o: give rich qualitative data about meanings
questions.why: Positivists favour quantitative methods such as surveys.

questions.q: A longitudinal study…
o: follows the same group over time
questions.why: It can show change and development.

questions.q: The Hawthorne effect is when…
o: people change behaviour because they know they are being studied
questions.why: It reduces the validity of observation.

questions.q: Why do interpretivists prefer participant observation?
o: It gives valid, in-depth understanding of meanings from the actor's view
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates gave strengths of participant observation alone rather than the interpretivist rationale.

questions.q: A researcher uses official crime statistics to compare regions. Why would interpretivists be cautious about this data?
o: It is too expensive to obtain
The samples are too small to generalise from
It is socially constructed by decisions about what to report and record
questions.why: Interpretivists see official statistics as the product of choices by the public and police, so they may not reflect the real amount of crime.

long.q: Explain two strengths of using participant observation in sociological research.
scheme: B1: a strength: high validity / rich qualitative data
B1: explained: the researcher sees behaviour in its natural setting and from the group's point of view (verstehen)
B1: a second strength: access to hidden or deviant groups
B1: explained: trust built over time lets the researcher see what interviews would miss

long.q: Explain the difference between reliability and validity in research.
scheme: B1: reliability: research that can be repeated with the same results
B1: e.g. standardised methods such as structured questionnaires are more reliable
B1: validity: research that gives a true picture of what it set out to study
B1: e.g. qualitative methods such as unstructured interviews are often more valid

long.q: Describe two ethical issues that sociologists must consider when carrying out research.
scheme: B1: informed consent
B1: described: participants should know the purpose of the research, agree to take part and be able to withdraw
B1: a second issue, e.g. confidentiality and anonymity, deception, or harm to participants
B1: described: e.g. names and identifying details kept private so participants cannot be traced

long.q: Explain the difference between positivist and interpretivist approaches to research.
scheme: B1: positivism: sociology should be scientific, studying social facts objectively
B1: positivists favour quantitative methods (questionnaires, structured interviews, official statistics) for reliability and generalisation
B1: example, e.g. Durkheim's use of official statistics to study suicide rates
B1: interpretivism: sociology should understand the meanings people give to their actions (verstehen, Weber)
B1: interpretivists favour qualitative methods (participant observation, unstructured interviews) for validity
B1: example, e.g. Atkinson's study of how coroners decide that a death is a suicide

long.q: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics in sociological research.
scheme: B1: strength: cheap and readily available secondary data
B1: strength: large-scale, allowing trends over time and comparisons between countries
B1: strength: often collected in standardised ways (e.g. a census), so reliable
B1: positivists value them for identifying patterns and correlations
B1: weakness: socially constructed by the decisions of officials, e.g. crime statistics miss unreported crime (the 'dark figure')
B1: weakness: definitions and collection methods change, making comparisons difficult
B1: weakness: no insight into meanings or motives (the interpretivist criticism)
B1: a judgement, e.g. useful for patterns but best combined with qualitative data (triangulation)

questions.q: A nuclear family consists of…
o: two parents and their dependent children
questions.why: Extended families include other relatives.

questions.q: Functionalists see the family as…
questions.why: Marxists and feminists offer critical views.

questions.q: Why is a reconstituted (step) family not automatically evidence of family diversity?
o: It is illegal in many countries
It can still be a nuclear family structure
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common misconception was that reconstituted families are an example of diversity, when they can still be nuclear.

questions.q: A question asks for the main reason for the increase in divorce. Which answer addresses it?
o: Changes in law and attitudes made divorce easier and more acceptable
questions.why: Examiners (2023): weak answers gave a reason why people divorce rather than why divorce has increased.

questions.q: Feminist sociologists note that women in full-time paid work often still do most of the housework and childcare. What is this called?
questions.why: The dual burden is the combination of paid work and most of the unpaid domestic labour, which challenges claims that roles have become equal.

long.q: Explain two ways in which family roles may have changed in modern industrial societies.
scheme: B1: one change, e.g. more symmetrical / joint conjugal roles
B1: explained, e.g. more women in paid work, men sharing domestic tasks (Young and Willmott)
B1: a second change, e.g. the 'dual burden' / changing children's roles / more lone-parent households
B1: explained with a reason or evidence

long.q: What is meant by the term 'beanpole family'?
scheme: B1: a multigenerational family that is 'long and thin': several generations, but few members in each generation
B1: caused by falling birth rates and rising life expectancy

long.q: Describe two reasons for the increase in divorce in many modern industrial societies.
scheme: B1: a reason, e.g. changes in the law
B1: described: divorce made cheaper and easier, e.g. 'no-fault' grounds
B1: a second reason, e.g. women's greater financial independence, or secularisation reducing stigma
B1: described: e.g. women in paid work are less likely to stay in an unhappy marriage for financial reasons

long.q: Explain how feminist sociologists view the family.
scheme: B1: the family is seen as patriarchal: it benefits men at women's expense
B1: liberal feminists: gradual progress towards equality through changing laws and attitudes
B1: Marxist feminists: women's unpaid domestic labour reproduces the workforce and benefits capitalism
B1: radical feminists: the family is a key source of patriarchy, e.g. domestic violence (Dobash and Dobash)
B1: evidence of continuing inequality, e.g. the dual burden or emotion work (Duncombe and Marsden)
B1: difference feminists: women's experiences of family vary by class, ethnicity and sexuality

long.q: Evaluate the view that childhood is socially constructed.
scheme: B1: meaning: childhood is defined by society rather than by biology, so it varies over time and between cultures
B1: historical evidence: Ariès argued that in medieval Europe children were treated as 'mini-adults'
B1: cross-cultural evidence: children in some societies take on work and responsibility early (e.g. Punch's study in rural Bolivia)
B1: modern laws construct childhood: compulsory schooling, child labour laws, age limits
B1: criticism: Ariès relied on limited evidence such as paintings; Pollock argued medieval parents did recognise childhood
B1: criticism: biological immaturity and dependence are universal
B1: Postman's 'disappearance of childhood' through media still supports the idea that childhood is constructed
B1: a reasoned judgement, e.g. biology sets limits, but the meaning and length of childhood are social

questions.q: The hidden curriculum is…
o: norms and values taught informally through school life
questions.why: For example, punctuality and obedience.

questions.q: Labelling theory in education suggests…
o: teachers' expectations can affect pupils' achievement
questions.why: It can create a self-fulfilling prophecy.

questions.q: A question asks how education 'legitimises' inequality. What must the answer focus on?
o: How education makes inequality seem fair and deserved (e.g. the myth of meritocracy)
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many ignored the key word 'legitimise' and only explained reproduction.

questions.q: Pupils placed in bottom sets form a group that rejects school values and gains status from misbehaving. What is this an example of?
questions.why: Labelled as failures, some pupils create an alternative status system that inverts school values, as interactionist studies of streaming have shown.

questions.q: What do Bowles and Gintis mean by the 'correspondence principle'?
o: School examinations correspond to pupils' real ability
Teachers' expectations correspond to pupils' results
Schools adapt to the culture of each pupil's home
Relationships in school mirror those of the capitalist workplace, preparing an obedient workforce
questions.why: These Marxists argue that hierarchy, rules and external rewards at school mirror work under capitalism, reproducing class inequality.

long.q: Explain how material deprivation may affect working-class students' achievement.
scheme: B1: lack of resources, e.g. books, devices, quiet space
B1: poor diet and housing affect health and attendance
B1: may need to work part-time / leave education early
B1: evidence or a sociologist, e.g. Douglas

long.q: Explain the functionalist view of the role of education.
scheme: B1: Durkheim: education transmits shared norms and values, creating social solidarity
B1: Durkheim: teaches specialist skills needed for a complex division of labour
B1: Parsons: school is a bridge from the family's particularistic values to society's universalistic standards
B1: Parsons: schools are meritocratic, so status is achieved, not ascribed
B1: Davis and Moore: role allocation, sifting and sorting the most able into the most important jobs
B1: education contributes to economic growth through human capital

long.q: Describe two ways in which the hidden curriculum may reinforce gender inequality.
scheme: B1: a way, e.g. teachers' different expectations and attention for boys and girls
B1: described: e.g. boys receive more attention in class discussion; girls are praised for neatness
B1: a second way, e.g. gendered subject choices and career advice
B1: described: e.g. girls steered away from physics and engineering, reinforcing gender segregation at work

long.q: Evaluate the view that ethnic differences in educational achievement are caused mainly by factors inside school.
scheme: B1: internal factor: teacher labelling and racism (e.g. Gillborn and Youdell on teachers' lower expectations of Black pupils)
B1: internal factor: an ethnocentric curriculum that marginalises minority cultures (e.g. Coard)
B1: internal factor: setting and streaming, and pupils' responses (e.g. Sewell's typology of Black male pupils)
B1: institutional racism in school policies (e.g. Gillborn)
B1: external factor: material deprivation linked to ethnicity
B1: external factors: cultural factors such as language and parental support (e.g. high achievement among Chinese and Indian pupils)
B1: evaluation: not all minority groups underachieve, so school racism alone cannot explain the pattern
B1: a reasoned judgement, e.g. internal and external factors interact, and ethnicity intersects with class and gender

long.q: Explain how Marxist sociologists see the relationship between education and the economy.
scheme: B1: education reproduces class inequality for the benefit of capitalism
B1: Bowles and Gintis: the correspondence principle, school mirrors the workplace
B1: the hidden curriculum teaches obedience and acceptance of hierarchy, producing a compliant workforce
B1: the 'myth of meritocracy' legitimises inequality, so failure is blamed on the individual
B1: Willis: working-class 'lads' reject school and so prepare themselves for manual work
B1: Bourdieu: middle-class cultural capital is rewarded, so class advantage passes between generations

questions.q: Cultural globalisation refers to…
o: the spread of ideas, values and media across the world
questions.why: Critics link it to cultural homogenisation.

questions.q: What is meant by globalisation?
o: The growing interconnection of societies through trade, communication and culture
Only the spread of the internet
questions.why: Consider economic, political and cultural globalisation.

questions.q: Which is a criticism of the view that globalisation creates one global culture?
questions.why: Hybrid cultures challenge the idea of a single culture.

questions.q: Which theory argues that poorer countries stay poor because wealthy countries exploit their cheap labour and raw materials?
questions.why: Dependency theory sees global inequality as the result of exploitation of the periphery by core nations, not of a lack of modern values.

questions.q: Migrants who keep close ties with their home country through social media, visits and sending money home, while living abroad, are best described as…
questions.why: Globalisation allows migrants to live across borders, keeping an identity and connections in more than one country.

long.q: What is meant by the term 'transnational corporation'?
scheme: B1: a company that produces or operates in many countries
B1: usually with headquarters in one country but production and markets spread worldwide (e.g. Unilever, Apple)

long.q: Describe two ways in which globalisation may affect people's identities.
scheme: B1: hybrid identities formed by mixing cultures through global media and migration
B1: described with an example, e.g. young people combining local traditions with global music and fashion
B1: resistance: a stronger local, national or religious identity in reaction to global culture
B1: described with an example, e.g. glocalisation, nationalist movements or religious revival

long.q: Explain how modernisation theory accounts for development.
scheme: B1: development is a process of moving from traditional to modern society, following the path of the West
B1: Rostow's stages of economic growth, from traditional society through 'take-off' to high mass consumption
B1: traditional values (fatalism, extended family obligations) are seen as barriers to development
B1: Western aid, investment and technology help countries reach 'take-off'
B1: cultural change through education, urbanisation and the media spreads modern values such as individualism and achievement
B1: criticism: ethnocentric, assumes Western capitalism is the only model (dependency theorists)

long.q: Evaluate the view that globalisation benefits developing countries.
scheme: B1: for: investment by transnational corporations brings jobs and economic growth
B1: for: examples such as the East Asian 'tiger' economies, or rapid poverty reduction in China
B1: for: technology transfer and access to global markets
B1: against: dependency and world-systems theory: exploitation of cheap labour, profits flow to the core
B1: against: poor working conditions, e.g. the Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh (2013)
B1: against: environmental damage, debt, cultural imperialism
B1: different perspectives compared, e.g. hyperglobalists, sceptics, transformationalists
B1: a reasoned judgement, e.g. benefits are uneven between countries and social groups

long.q: Explain two ways in which migration is linked to globalisation.
scheme: B1: economic migration from poorer to richer countries within a global labour market
B1: explained: e.g. remittances sent home become a major source of income for some countries
B1: transnational communities and diasporas kept together by cheap travel and digital communication
B1: explained: e.g. the feminisation of migration in 'global care chains' (women migrating as care and domestic workers)

questions.q: Agenda setting means the media…
o: influences which issues people think about
questions.why: Choosing what to cover shapes public priorities.

questions.q: What does the pluralist view say about media content?
o: It is controlled by the ruling class
It reflects audience demand and a variety of views
It is controlled by the state
questions.why: Marxists argue owners control content.

questions.q: What is the hypodermic syringe model?
o: Audiences choose and interpret media actively
questions.why: Uses and gratifications and two-step flow see audiences as more active.

questions.q: A study finds that news coverage of strikes focuses on disruption to the public and gives more air time to management than to workers. Which view of the media does this support?
questions.why: Neo-Marxists argue that journalists' shared middle-class assumptions lead news to reflect dominant ideas, so workers' views are marginalised.

questions.q: Which claim about new media is most consistent with a pluralist view?
o: New media let ordinary people create and share content, weakening the control of traditional owners
A few technology companies now control what most people see
New media spread capitalist ideology more effectively than before
New media make audiences more passive
questions.why: Pluralists stress diversity and audience power; citizen journalism and user-generated content fit that view, while the others are Marxist or critical claims.

long.q: Assess the view that the media set the agenda for public debate.
scheme: B1: agenda-setting: the media choose what is newsworthy (gatekeeping)
B1: evidence, e.g. news values (Galtung and Ruge)
B1: counter: audiences are active; social media lets the public set agendas
B1: a supported judgement

long.q: Describe two ways in which ownership may influence media content.
scheme: B1: direct influence of owners (proprietors) on the editorial line
B1: described: e.g. owners appoint like-minded editors, so news reflects their political views
B1: commercial pressures from advertisers and the need for profit
B1: described: e.g. content that might offend advertisers is avoided; cheap, popular content is favoured

long.q: Explain the uses and gratifications approach to the media.
scheme: B1: audiences are active: they choose media to satisfy their own needs, rather than being passively affected
B1: diversion: media used for escape and entertainment
B1: personal relationships: companionship, e.g. viewers relating to characters or presenters
B1: personal identity: comparing oneself with people in the media
B1: surveillance: finding out what is happening in the world (news)
B1: criticism: exaggerates audience choice and ignores how the media shape people's needs

long.q: Evaluate the view that the media represent ethnic minorities in stereotypical ways.
scheme: B1: evidence: news links minorities with crime, conflict and social problems (e.g. Van Dijk)
B1: moral panics about minority groups, e.g. Hall et al. on the 'mugging' panic of the 1970s
B1: under-representation or narrow roles in mainstream media (symbolic annihilation)
B1: explanations: news values and dominant ideology (Marxist / neo-Marxist)
B1: counter: increasing diversity in programmes, presenters and characters
B1: counter: new media let minority groups produce their own content
B1: counter: audiences interpret content actively and may reject stereotypes
B1: a reasoned judgement, e.g. stereotyping persists, especially in news, but representation is changing

long.q: Explain how the 'digital divide' affects access to new media.
scheme: B1: the digital divide: the gap between those who have access to digital technology and the skills to use it and those who do not
B1: social class and income: the cost of devices and broadband
B1: age: older people may lack digital skills or confidence
B1: global and rural divides: weak infrastructure in some regions and countries

questions.q: Secularisation is…
o: the decline in the social significance of religion
questions.why: Debates focus on how to measure it.

questions.q: What is secularisation?
o: The process by which religion loses social significance
questions.why: Evidence: falling attendance, but beliefs may continue privately.

questions.q: Which view sees religion as promoting social solidarity?
questions.why: Marxists see religion as ideology that keeps the poor passive.

questions.q: Weber's study of the 'Protestant ethic' is used to argue that religion can…
o: be a force for social change
have no effect on economic life
questions.why: Weber argued that Calvinist beliefs encouraged hard work and saving, which helped the development of capitalism.

questions.q: Many people say they hold religious beliefs but rarely attend a place of worship. What does this suggest about the evidence for secularisation?
o: Attendance figures prove religion is growing
Belief has fallen faster than attendance
Falling attendance may exaggerate decline, as religion becomes more private ('believing without belonging')
questions.why: If belief persists while attendance falls, measuring religion by attendance alone may overstate secularisation.

long.q: What is meant by the term 'religious fundamentalism'?
scheme: B1: a return to what are seen as the basic, literal truths of a religion's sacred texts
B1: often a reaction against modernity and secularisation, rejecting liberal values

long.q: Describe two functions of religion according to functionalists.
scheme: B1: social solidarity (Durkheim)
B1: described: collective worship of sacred symbols binds people to shared values
B1: helping people cope with life crises (Malinowski), or providing meaning and values (Parsons)
B1: described: e.g. rituals at death reduce anxiety and restore social stability

long.q: Explain the Marxist view of religion.
scheme: B1: religion is part of the superstructure and spreads ruling-class ideology
B1: Marx: religion is the 'opium of the people', dulling the pain of exploitation
B1: promises of reward in the afterlife discourage revolution in this life
B1: religion legitimises inequality, e.g. the divine right of kings
B1: it creates false consciousness among the working class
B1: neo-Marxists, e.g. Maduro: religion can be relatively autonomous and support change (liberation theology)

long.q: Evaluate the claim that secularisation is taking place in modern societies.
scheme: B1: for: declining church attendance and membership in much of Western Europe
B1: for: rationalisation and 'disenchantment' (Weber; Bruce)
B1: for: structural differentiation: religion loses functions to other institutions (Parsons)
B1: against: 'believing without belonging' (Davie): belief persists without attendance
B1: against: growth of new religious movements and spirituality (e.g. Heelas and Woodhead)
B1: against: religion is growing in the Global South and remains strong in the USA; rise of fundamentalism
B1: problems of measurement: definitions of religion and reliability of attendance data
B1: a reasoned judgement, e.g. religion is changing form rather than simply declining, and the picture varies by region

long.q: Explain two ways in which religion may act as a force for social change.
scheme: B1: Weber: the Protestant ethic
B1: explained: Calvinist values of hard work and saving helped bring about the rise of capitalism
B1: religious movements supporting change, e.g. Black churches in the US civil rights movement, or liberation theology in Latin America
B1: explained: churches gave organisation, leadership and moral legitimacy to campaigns (e.g. Bruce)
